title: Borrowed APIs that Unconditionally Copy into Ownership
pattern: An API accepts borrowed data (`&T`, `&str`, `&[T]`) but immediately allocates an owned copy (`.clone()`, `.to_string()`, `.to_owned()`, `.to_vec()`) on every call, denying callers the option to move an existing owned value.
why_bad: The signature hides a heap allocation and memory copy on every call and prevents callers from reusing ownership they already have, even when they hold a temporary `String` or `Vec<T>` they could have moved. It strips the caller of allocator control and cost visibility, making high-frequency loops or bulk operations needlessly expensive, often just to keep the signature free of lifetime annotations.
detection: Either of: (1) a parameter taken by reference (`&String`, `&Vec<T>`, `&[T]`, `&str`) is cloned or converted to an owned type immediately in the function body, without semantic mutation of the underlying shared structure; or (2) a public constructor or builder method accepts a reference type and immediately copies it into an owned struct field without providing an alternative owned consuming constructor.
counterexample: The struct genuinely holds a borrow and lifetimes are intended to restrict its scope; ownership is only needed conditionally under rare branches (e.g., error recovery, logging, dynamic format changes); or the copy cost is documented and demonstrably negligible and ergonomics is the overriding concern. Owning a struct field is not itself a smell. Mark `Context-dependent`.
source: *Rust For Rustaceans*, Chapter 3, "Ownership" (p. 41-42 / 435-436); Jon Gjengset, *Rust for Rustaceans*, Chapter 4, "Ownership" (p. 23, 26).
